Detailed Description

◆ abs()

template<typename ExType >
static ExType casadi::GenericExpression< ExType >::abs ( const ExType &  x)
inlinestatic

Elementwise; structural zeros are preserved. The unary functions of this group operate on every entry, keep the shape and build a symbolic expression for SX and MX. Those that map 0 to 0 (abs, sqrt, sin, tan, atan, asin, sinh, tanh, asinh, atanh, floor, ceil, sign, erf, erfinv, log1p, expm1) keep the sparsity pattern; the others (cos, cosh, exp, log, log10, acos, acosh, logic_not) return a dense result. Named fabs in Python, where the built-in abs also applies.

>>> fabs(DM([-1, 0, 2]))
DM([1, 0, 2])
>>> fabs(DM.eye(2) * -1)
DM(
[[1, 00],
 [00, 1]])
>>> abs(SX.sym("x"))
SX(fabs(x))


>> abs(DM([-1; 0; 2]))
[1, 0, 2]
>> abs(-DM.eye(2))
[[1, 00],
 [00, 1]]
>> abs(SX.sym('x'))
fabs(x)


julia> abs.(ca.DM([-1, 0, 2]))
DM([1, 0, 2])
julia> abs(-ca.DM.eye(2))
DM(
[[1, 00],
 [00, 1]])
julia> abs(ca.SX.sym("x"))
SX(fabs(x))

See also
sign, copysign

◆ atan2()

template<typename ExType >
static ExType casadi::GenericExpression< ExType >::atan2 ( const ExType &  y,
const ExType &  x 
)
inlinestatic

theta = atan2(y,x) corresponds to x = r cos(theta), y = r sin(theta)

Angle in (-pi, pi] of the point (x, y), taking the quadrant into account; the first argument is the y coordinate, as in C and numpy. Elementwise, shape rules as for plus. atan2(0, 0) is 0.

◆ bilin()

template<typename MatType >
static MatType casadi::GenericMatrix< MatType >::bilin ( const MatType &  A,
const MatType &  x,
const MatType &  y 
)
static

x and y must be vectors (row vectors are transposed, sparse vectors densified) with x.numel() == A.size1() and y.numel() == A.size2(); otherwise an error is raised. The result is scalar. When y is omitted, the quadratic form x^T A x is calculated.

>>> A = DM([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
>>> bilin(A, DM([1, 1]), DM([1, 2]))
DM(16)
>>> bilin(A, DM([1, 1]))
DM(10)
>>> bilin(MX.sym("A", 2, 2), MX.sym("x", 2), MX.sym("y", 2))
MX(bilin(A, x, y))


>> A = DM([1 2; 3 4]);
>> bilin(A, DM([1; 1]), DM([1; 2]))
16
>> bilin(A, DM([1; 1]))
10
>> bilin(MX.sym('A', 2, 2), MX.sym('x', 2), MX.sym('y', 2))
bilin(A, x, y)


julia> A = ca.DM([1 2; 3 4]);
julia> ca.bilin(A, ca.DM([1, 1]), ca.DM([1, 2]))
DM(16)
julia> ca.bilin(A, ca.DM([1, 1]))
DM(10)
julia> ca.bilin(ca.MX.sym("A", 2, 2), ca.MX.sym("x", 2), ca.MX.sym("y", 2))
MX(bilin(A, x, y))

See also
rank1, dot, mtimes

◆ constpow()

template<typename ExType >
static ExType casadi::GenericExpression< ExType >::constpow ( const ExType &  x,
const ExType &  y 
)
inlinestatic

Same value as pow, but the exponent is assumed constant: the derivative with respect to y is taken as zero. pow itself produces this operation for a non-integer constant exponent, so it is rarely needed directly. Passing a symbolic exponent gives a wrong derivative for MX; SX falls back to pow.

>>> constpow(DM(2), 3)
DM(8)
>>> x = MX.sym("x")
>>> constpow(x, 2.5), jacobian(constpow(x, 2.5), x)
(MX(pow(x,2.5)), MX((2.5*pow(x,1.5))))


>> constpow(DM(2), 3)
8
>> x = MX.sym('x');
>> constpow(x, 2.5), jacobian(constpow(x, 2.5), x)
pow(x,2.5)
(2.5*pow(x,1.5))


julia> ca.constpow(ca.DM(2), 3)
DM(8)
julia> x = ca.MX.sym("x");
julia> ca.constpow(x, 2.5), ca.jacobian(ca.constpow(x, 2.5), x)
(pow(x,2.5), (2.5*pow(x,1.5)))

See also
pow

◆ eq()

template<typename ExType >
static ExType casadi::GenericExpression< ExType >::eq ( const ExType &  x,
const ExType &  y 
)
inlinestatic

Elementwise comparison with 0/1 result, see lt: this is value equality of the entries, not identity of expressions; use is_equal to test whether two symbolic expressions are the same. For symbolic operands x == x with the same node simplifies to 1. NaN is not equal to anything, including itself.

>>> eq(DM([1, 2, 3]), 2)
DM([0, 1, 0])
>>> DM.eye(2) == DM([[1, 0], [0, 1]])
DM(
[[1, 1],
 [1, 1]])
>>> x = SX.sym("x")
>>> x == x, x == SX.sym("x")
(SX(1), SX((x==x)))
>>> DM(float("nan")) == DM(float("nan"))
DM(0)


>> eq(DM([1; 2; 3]), 2)
[0, 1, 0]
>> DM.eye(2) == DM([1 0; 0 1])
[[1, 1],
 [1, 1]]
>> x = SX.sym('x');
>> x == x, x == SX.sym('x')
1
(x==x)
>> DM(nan) == DM(nan)
0


julia> ca.eq(ca.DM([1, 2, 3]), 2)
DM([0, 1, 0])
julia> ca.DM.eye(2) == ca.DM([1 0; 0 1])
DM(
[[1, 1],
 [1, 1]])
julia> x = ca.SX.sym("x");
julia> x == x, x == ca.SX.sym("x")
(1, (x==x))
julia> ca.DM(NaN) == ca.DM(NaN)
DM(0)

ne, is_equal

Elementwise maximum; shape rules as for plus. Follows C fmax: when one operand is NaN the other is returned. The derivative is 1 with respect to the larger operand (split evenly on ties). For the maximum over the entries of one matrix use mmax.

>>> fmax(DM([1, 5]), DM([3, 2]))
DM([3, 5])
>>> fmax(DM([1, 5]), 3)
DM([3, 5])
>>> fmax(DM([1, float("nan")]), DM([float("nan"), 2]))
DM([1, 2])
>>> fmax(MX.sym("x"), MX.sym("y"))
MX(fmax(x,y))


>> fmax(DM([1; 5]), DM([3; 2]))
[3, 5]
>> max(DM([1; 5]), 3)
[3, 5]
>> fmax(DM([1; nan]), DM([nan; 2]))
[1, 2]
>> max(MX.sym('x'), MX.sym('y'))
fmax(x,y)


julia> max.(ca.DM([1, 5]), ca.DM([3, 2]))
DM([3, 5])
julia> max.(ca.DM([1, 5]), 3)
DM([3, 5])
julia> max.(ca.DM([1, NaN]), ca.DM([NaN, 2]))
DM([1, 2])
julia> max(ca.MX.sym("x"), ca.MX.sym("y"))

◆ fmin()

template<typename ExType >
static ExType casadi::GenericExpression< ExType >::fmin ( const ExType &  x,
const ExType &  y 
)
inlinestatic

Elementwise minimum; shape rules as for plus. Follows C fmin: when one operand is NaN the other is returned, NaN results only when both are NaN. The derivative is 1 with respect to the smaller operand (split evenly on ties). The sparsity pattern is kept where both operands are structurally zero; fmin with a negative scalar densifies. For the minimum over the entries of one matrix use mmin.

>>> fmin(DM([1, 5]), DM([3, 2]))
DM([1, 2])
>>> fmin(DM([1, float("nan")]), DM([float("nan"), 2]))
DM([1, 2])
>>> fmin(DM.eye(2), 1)
DM(
[[1, 00],
 [00, 1]])
>>> fmin(SX.sym("x"), SX.sym("y"))
SX(fmin(x,y))


>> fmin(DM([1; 5]), DM([3; 2]))
[1, 2]
>> min(DM([1; 5]), DM([3; 2]))
[1, 2]
>> fmin(DM([1; nan]), DM([nan; 2]))
[1, 2]
>> fmin(DM.eye(2), 1)
[[1, 00],
 [00, 1]]
>> min(SX.sym('x'), SX.sym('y'))
fmin(x,y)


julia> min.(ca.DM([1, 5]), ca.DM([3, 2]))
DM([1, 2])
julia> min.(ca.DM([1, NaN]), ca.DM([NaN, 2]))

◆ if_else_zero()

template<typename ExType >
static ExType casadi::GenericExpression< ExType >::if_else_zero ( const ExType &  x,
const ExType &  y 
)
inlinestatic

Elementwise: y where x is nonzero, 0 elsewhere; the result is structurally zero wherever either operand is. The value of y in the inactive branch does not propagate, so a NaN or inf there yields 0 rather than NaN, and the derivatives are treated accordingly. This is the building block of if_else; it is not exposed as a function in Python, use if_else(x, y, 0) there.

◆ logic_and()

template<typename ExType >
static ExType casadi::GenericExpression< ExType >::logic_and ( const ExType &  x,
const ExType &  y 
)
inlinestatic

Returns (an expression evaluating to) 1 where both entries are nonzero and 0 otherwise, elementwise

Any nonzero value, including NaN, counts as true. Shape rules as for plus; the result is structurally zero wherever either operand is. The Python keyword and does not work on matrices (it needs a single truth value); use this function.

 >>> logic_and(DM([1, 2, 0]), DM([3, 0, 0]))
 DM([1, 0, 0])
 >>> logic_and(SX.sym("x"), SX.sym("y"))
 SX((x&&y))
 >>> logic_and(DM.eye(2), DM.ones(2, 2))
 DM(
 [[1, 00],
  [00, 1]])

 [1, 0, 0]
 >> SX.sym('x') & SX.sym('y')
 (x&&y)
 >> and(DM.eye(2), DM.ones(2, 2))
 [[1, 00],
  [00, 1]]

 julia> ca.logic_and(ca.DM([1, 2, 0]), ca.DM([3, 0, 0]))
 DM([1, 0, 0])
 julia> ca.logic_and(ca.SX.sym("x"), ca.SX.sym("y"))
 SX((x&&y))
 julia> ca.logic_and(ca.DM.eye(2), ca.DM.ones(2, 2))

template<typename ExType >

inlinestatic

Elementwise comparison; shape rules as for plus. Every comparison in this group returns a matrix of the same type as the operands with entries 1 (true) and 0 (false): for DM a numeric 0/1 matrix, not a boolean, and for SX and MX a symbolic expression that is only decided at evaluation time. Comparisons with NaN are false. The result is sparse where both operands are structurally zero (0 < 0 is false).

>>> lt(DM([1, 2, 3]), 2)

>>> DM([1, 2, 3]) < DM([3, 2, 1])

>>> DM.eye(2) < 1

 [1, 0]])

◆ mod()

template<typename ExType >
static ExType casadi::GenericExpression< ExType >::mod ( const ExType &  x,
const ExType &  y 
)
inlinestatic

This Function follows the convention of https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/numeric/math/fmod: the result has the sign of x and magnitude below |y|.

This is equivalent to Python's numpy.fmod and Matlab's rem. It differs from the Python operator x % y on these objects, which follows the Python convention x - y*floor(x/y) (result with the sign of y). Elementwise, shape rules as for plus; structural zeros of x stay zero. A zero divisor gives NaN.

>>> fmod(DM([5, 5, -5, -5]), DM([3, -3, 3, -3]))
DM([2, 2, -2, -2])
>>> DM([5, 5, -5, -5]) % DM([3, -3, 3, -3])
DM([2, -1, 1, -2])
>>> fmod(SX.sym("x"), 2), SX.sym("x") % 2
(SX(fmod(x,2)), SX((x-(2.*floor((x/2))))))


>> x = DM([5; 5; -5; -5]); y = DM([3; -3; 3; -3]);
>> fmod(x, y)
[2, 2, -2, -2]
>> rem(x, y)
[2, 2, -2, -2]
>> x - y .* floor(x ./ y)
[2, -1, 1, -2]
>> rem(SX.sym('x'), 2)
fmod(x,2)


julia> ca.fmod(ca.DM([5, 5, -5, -5]), ca.DM([3, -3, 3, -3]))
DM([2, 2, -2, -2])
julia> mod.(ca.DM([5, 5, -5, -5]), ca.DM([3, -3, 3, -3]))
DM([2, -1, 1, -2])
julia> ca.fmod(ca.SX.sym("x"), 2)
SX(fmod(x,2))

See also
remainder, floor

◆ plus()

template<typename ExType >
static ExType casadi::GenericExpression< ExType >::plus ( const ExType &  x,
const ExType &  y 
)
inlinestatic

Elementwise sum. The shape rules below hold for every binary operation in this group (minus, times, rdivide, the comparisons, logic_and, ...):

  • both operands have the same shape, or
  • one operand is a scalar (1-by-1), which is combined with every element, or
  • the operands have the same number of rows and the column count of one is a multiple of the other's; the narrower one is repeated horizontally (so a column vector can be added to every column of a matrix, but a row vector cannot be added to every row). Any other combination raises an error; there is no further broadcasting. Empty matrices follow the same rules and give an empty result.

The result is sparse where both operands are structurally zero; an entry that is a structural zero in only one operand becomes an explicit value. Operations that map (0, y) or (x, 0) to a nonzero, such as x + 1 or cos, densify the result. Numeric (DM) operands are evaluated, symbolic ones (SX, MX) build an expression; DM and SX or MX can be mixed, SX and MX cannot.

>>> plus(DM([1, 2]), DM([10, 20]))
DM([11, 22])
>>> DM([1, 2]) + 1
DM([2, 3])
>>> DM.eye(2) + DM.eye(2)
DM(
[[2, 00],
 [00, 2]])
>>> DM.eye(2) + 1
DM(
[[2, 1],
 [1, 2]])
>>> SX.sym("x", 2, 2) + SX.sym("y", 2)
SX(
[[(x_0+y_0), (x_2+y_0)],
 [(x_1+y_1), (x_3+y_1)]])
>>> (MX.sym("x", 2, 0) + 1).shape
(2, 0)
>>> DM.ones(2, 2) + DM.ones(1, 2)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
RuntimeError: ...Dimension mismatch...

Elementwise; shape rules as for plus. Named power in Python, where the ** operator maps to it as well. A constant exponent is simplified symbolically: integer powers become repeated squaring and multiplication, 0.5 becomes sqrt, -1 a reciprocal, other constants a constpow operation. ◆ printme()

template<typename ExType >
static ExType casadi::GenericExpression< ExType >::printme ( const ExType &  x,
const ExType &  y 
)
inlinestatic

Identity operation with a side effect: whenever the expression is evaluated inside a Function (and hence inside a solver), every nonzero of x is printed on its own line as "|> y : value" in storage (column-major) order, with y an identifier of choice to tell several printme nodes apart. Available as a method x.printme(y) in Python; the derivative is that of x. Use monitor to print a whole matrix at once.

>>> x = MX.sym("x")
>>> f = Function("f", [x], [x.printme(7) * 2])
>>> f(3)
|> 7 : 3.0000000000000000e+00
DM(6)


>> x = MX.sym('x');
>> f = Function('f', {x}, {x.printme(7) * 2});
>> f(3)
|> 7 : 3.0000000000000000e+00
6


julia> x = ca.MX.sym("x");
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [x], [ca.printme(x, 7) * 2]);
julia> f(3)
|> 7 : 3.0000000000000000e+00
DM(6)

◆ remainder()

template<typename ExType >
static ExType casadi::GenericExpression< ExType >::remainder ( const ExType &  x,
const ExType &  y 
)
inlinestatic

This Function follows the convention of https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/numeric/math/remainder: x - n*y with n the integer nearest to x/y (ties to even), so the result lies in [-|y|/2, |y|/2].

Notably:

  • remainder(5,3) -> -1
  • remainder(5,-3) -> -1
  • remainder(-5,3) -> 1
  • remainder(-5,-3) -> 1

This is equivalent to Python's math.remainder. There is no equivalence in Matlab. Elementwise, shape rules as for plus; structural zeros of x stay zero.

>>> remainder(DM([5, 5, -5, -5]), DM([3, -3, 3, -3]))
DM([-1, -1, 1, 1])
>>> remainder(DM([2.5, 3.5]), 2)
DM([0.5, -0.5])
>>> remainder(MX.sym("x"), 2)
MX(remainder(x,2))


>> remainder(DM([5; 5; -5; -5]), DM([3; -3; 3; -3]))
[-1, -1, 1, 1]
>> remainder(DM([2.5; 3.5]), 2)
[0.5, -0.5]
>> remainder(MX.sym('x'), 2)
remainder(x,2)


julia> ca.remainder(ca.DM([5, 5, -5, -5]), ca.DM([3, -3, 3, -3]))
DM([-1, -1, 1, 1])
julia> ca.remainder(ca.DM([2.5, 3.5]), 2)
DM([0.5, -0.5])
julia> ca.remainder(ca.MX.sym("x"), 2)
MX(remainder(x,2))

◆ abs

template<typename ExType >
ExType abs ( const ExType &  x)
friend

Elementwise; structural zeros are preserved. The unary functions of this group operate on every entry, keep the shape and build a symbolic expression for SX and MX. Those that map 0 to 0 (abs, sqrt, sin, tan, atan, asin, sinh, tanh, asinh, atanh, floor, ceil, sign, erf, erfinv, log1p, expm1) keep the sparsity pattern; the others (cos, cosh, exp, log, log10, acos, acosh, logic_not) return a dense result. Named fabs in Python, where the built-in abs also applies.

>>> fabs(DM([-1, 0, 2]))
DM([1, 0, 2])
>>> fabs(DM.eye(2) * -1)
DM(
[[1, 00],
 [00, 1]])
>>> abs(SX.sym("x"))
SX(fabs(x))


>> abs(DM([-1; 0; 2]))
[1, 0, 2]
>> abs(-DM.eye(2))
[[1, 00],
 [00, 1]]
>> abs(SX.sym('x'))
fabs(x)


julia> abs.(ca.DM([-1, 0, 2]))
DM([1, 0, 2])
julia> abs(-ca.DM.eye(2))
DM(
[[1, 00],
 [00, 1]])
julia> abs(ca.SX.sym("x"))

sign, copysign

◆ adj

template<typename Scalar >
Matrix<Scalar> adj ( const Matrix< Scalar > &  A)
friend

Transpose of the cofactor matrix, computed by Laplace expansion. For an invertible matrix inv(A) == adj(A)/det(A). Cost grows factorially with the size; intended for small (symbolic) matrices. A structural zero cofactor stays structurally zero. A non-square input raises an error.

>>> adj(DM([[1, 2], [3, 4]]))
DM(
[[4, -2],
 [-3, 1]])
>>> X = SX.sym("X", 2, 2)
>>> adj(X)
SX(

>>> adj(DM(5)), adj(DM(Sparsity.diag(3))).nnz()
(DM(1), 3)

◆ blockcat [2/2]

template<typename MatType >
MatType blockcat ( const std::vector< std::vector< MatType > > &  v)
friend

Each inner list is a block row: its entries are concatenated horizontally, and the resulting block rows are concatenated vertically. The usual concatenation rules apply: blocks in one block row need the same number of rows, block rows need the same total number of columns, otherwise an error is raised. Inverse of blocksplit: blockcat(blocksplit(x, ...)) == x.

Parameters
vList of block rows, each a list of matrices
Returns
Matrix of the same type as the blocks

>>> blockcat([[DM(1), DM([[2, 3]])], [DM([4, 5]), DM.eye(2)]])
DM(
[[1, 2, 3],
 [4, 1, 00],
 [5, 00, 1]])
>>> a, b, c, d = MX.sym("a", 2, 2), MX.sym("b", 2, 1), MX.sym("c", 1, 2), MX.sym("d")

◆ bspline [1/3]

MX bspline ( const MX &  x,
const DM &  coeffs,
const std::vector< std::vector< double > > &  knots,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  degree,
casadi_int  m,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
)
friend

Returns an m-by-1 expression with the spline values at x. The spline is defined by one knot vector and one degree per dimension; the number of basis functions per dimension is len(knots[i]) - degree[i] - 1 and the coefficient vector must hold m times the product of these counts, in column-major order. Outside the knot range the spline is zero. Derivatives are available.

Parameters
xColumn vector with one entry per dimension
coeffsCoefficient vector; its length is not validated
knotsOne knot vector per dimension, numeric
degreeDegree per dimension; must have as many entries as knots
mNumber of outputs per evaluation
opts"lookup_mode" (see low) and "inline" (bool, default false: build an explicit expression instead of a BSpline node). Unknown keys are ignored.

>>> x = MX.sym("x")
>>> knots = [[0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3]]
>>> c = DM(range(6))
>>> y = bspline(x, c, knots, [3], 1)
>>> f = Function("f", [x], [y])
>>> y, f(1.5), f(4)
(MX(BSpline(x)), DM(2.5), DM(0))
>>> Function("df", [x], [jacobian(y, x)])(1.5)
DM(1.125)
>>> try:
...   bspline(MX.sym("v", 2), c, knots, [3], 1)
... except Exception as e:
...   print("must match" in str(e))
True


>> x = MX.sym('x');
>> knots = {[0 0 0 0 1 2 3 3 3 3]};
>> c = DM((0:5)');
>> y = bspline(x, c, knots, 3, 1);
>> f = Function('f', {x}, {y});
>> y, f(1.5), f(4)
BSpline(x)
2.5
0
>> df = Function('df', {x}, {jacobian(y, x)});
>> df(1.5)
1.125
>> try, bspline(MX.sym('v', 2), c, knots, 3, 1); catch e, disp('must match'); end
must match


julia> x = ca.MX.sym("x");
julia> knots = [[0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3]];
julia> c = ca.DM(0:5);
julia> y = ca.bspline(x, c, knots, [3], 1);
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [x], [y]);
julia> y, f(1.5), f(4)
(BSpline(x), 2.5, 0)
julia> ca.Function("df", [x], [ca.jacobian(y, x)])(1.5)
DM(1.125)
julia> try
           ca.bspline(ca.MX.sym("v", 2), c, knots, [3], 1)
       catch e
           println(occursin("must match", sprint(showerror, e)))
       end
true

◆ chol

template<typename Scalar >
Matrix<Scalar> chol ( const Matrix< Scalar > &  A)
friend

Returns the upper triangular factor R with R^T*R == A, obtained from the sparse LDL^T factorization (without fill-reducing permutation) as diag(sqrt(D))*L^T. The sparsity pattern of A must be symmetric; otherwise an error is raised. An indefinite A gives nan entries without an error. Works symbolically on SX.

template<typename MatType >

If the scalar condition ind evaluates to the integer k, where 0<=k<x.size(), then x[k] is returned, otherwise x_default is returned (also for negative or non-integer values). By default this is a chain of if_else expressions, so all cases are evaluated. With short_circuit true (MX only; SX raises an error) a Switch function evaluates only the selected case.

>>> X = MX.sym("X"); Y = MX.sym("Y")
>>> conditional(X, [Y, 2*Y], 0, True)

◆ convexify

MX convexify ( const MX &  H,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
)
friend

Returns an expression with the sparsity pattern of H that, when evaluated, modifies the value of H so that it is positive definite. Intended for Hessians in SQP-type methods. H must be square and symmetric or triangular (a triangular pattern is interpreted as one half of a symmetric matrix); other patterns raise an error. The node has no derivatives.

Parameters
HSquare expression with a symmetric or triangular sparsity pattern
optsOptions: "strategy": "eigen-clip" (default, eigenvalues below the margin are set to the margin), "eigen-reflect" (their absolute value is taken) or "regularize" (a multiple of the identity is added; symmetric patterns only); "margin": smallest allowed eigenvalue, default 1e-7, must be nonnegative; "max_iter_eig": iteration limit of the eigenvalue computation, default 200; "verbose": print the block structure found. Unknown keys raise an error.

>>> H = MX.sym("H", 2, 2)
>>> f = Function("f", [H], [convexify(H)])
>>> f(DM([[1, 0], [0, -2]]))
DM(
[[1, 0],
 [0, 1e-07]])
>>> f = Function("f", [H], [convexify(H, {"strategy": "eigen-reflect"})])
>>> f(DM([[1, 0], [0, -2]]))
DM(
[[1, 0],
 [0, 2]])
>>> f = Function("f", [H], [convexify(H, {"strategy": "regularize", "margin": 0.5})])
>>> f(DM([[1, 0], [0, -2]]))
DM(
[[3.5, 0],
 [0, 0.5]])
>>> try:
...   convexify(H, {"strategy": "foo"})
... except Exception as e:
...   print("Invalid convexify strategy" in str(e))
True


>> H = MX.sym('H', 2, 2);
>> f = Function('f', {H}, {convexify(H)});
>> f(DM([1 0; 0 -2]))
[[1, 0],
 [0, 1e-07]]
>> f = Function('f', {H}, {convexify(H, struct('strategy', 'eigen-reflect'))});
>> f(DM([1 0; 0 -2]))
[[1, 0],
 [0, 2]]
>> f = Function('f', {H}, {convexify(H, struct('strategy', 'regularize', 'margin', 0.5))});
>> f(DM([1 0; 0 -2]))
[[3.5, 0],
 [0, 0.5]]
>> try, convexify(H, struct('strategy', 'foo')); catch e, disp('invalid strategy'); end
invalid strategy


julia> H = ca.MX.sym("H", 2, 2);
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [H], [ca.convexify(H)]);
julia> print(f([1 0; 0 -2]))
[[1, 0],
 [0, 1e-07]]
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [H], [ca.convexify(H, Dict("strategy" => "eigen-reflect"))]);

◆ depends_on

template<typename MatType >
bool depends_on ( const MatType &  f,
const MatType &  arg 
)
friend

The argument must be symbolic (for MX: symbolic primitives as created by MX.sym, not elements of them).

The dependency is in a mathematical way: Does the value of the argument affect the value of the expression? Equivalently, will the corresponding entry of the Jacobian by a non-zero? This is decided by sparsity propagation through the graph, so 0*x and x-x do not depend on x.

The symbol could still be present in the expression graph.

To check that kind of dependency, use contains(symvar(f),arg)

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y")
>>> depends_on(x*y, x), depends_on(x*y, SX.sym("z"))
(True, False)
>>> depends_on(0*x, x), depends_on(x - x, x), depends_on(SX(3), x)
(False, False, False)
>>> depends_on(vertcat(x, 3), vertcat(x, y))
True
>>> v = MX.sym("v", 2)
>>> depends_on(v[0], v)
True


>> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y');
>> fprintf('%d %d\n', depends_on(x*y, x), depends_on(x*y, SX.sym('z')))
1 0
>> fprintf('%d %d %d\n', depends_on(0*x, x), depends_on(x - x, x), depends_on(SX(3), x))
0 0 0
>> depends_on(vertcat(x, 3), vertcat(x, y))
1
>> v = MX.sym('v', 2);
>> depends_on(v(1), v)
1


julia> x = ca.SX.sym("x"); y = ca.SX.sym("y");
julia> ca.depends_on(x * y, x), ca.depends_on(x * y, ca.SX.sym("z"))
(true, false)
julia> ca.depends_on(0 * x, x), ca.depends_on(x - x, x), ca.depends_on(ca.SX(3), x)
(false, false, false)
julia> ca.depends_on([x; 3], [x; y])
true
julia> v = ca.MX.sym("v", 2);
julia> ca.depends_on(v[1], v)
true

See also
which_depends, symvar, contains, jacobian_sparsity

friend

For DM and SX the determinant is formed by minor expansion along the sparsest row or column (a 2-by-2 directly, a scalar is returned as is); the cost grows quickly with the matrix size. ◆ diagsplit [4/4]

template<typename MatType >
std::vector< MatType > diagsplit ( const MatType &  x,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  output_offset1,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  output_offset2 
)
friend

Block i is x[output_offset1[i]:output_offset1[i+1], output_offset2[i]:output_offset2[i+1]]. Both lists must have the same length, start at 0, be non-decreasing and end at the row (column) count of x. Entries of x outside the diagonal blocks must be zero (structurally zero for MX and Sparsity), otherwise an error is raised. Inverse of diagcat: diagcat(diagsplit(x, ...)) == x for block-diagonal x.

Parameters
xMatrix (or Sparsity) to split; any shape
output_offset1Row boundaries of the blocks
output_offset2Column boundaries of the blocks
Returns
List of matrices of the same type as x, one per block

>>> x = DM([[1, 2, 0], [0, 0, 6]])
>>> diagsplit(x, [0, 1, 2], [0, 2, 3])

Each pass subtracts neighbouring rows (axis 0) or columns (axis 1), shrinking that dimension by one; n passes are applied. With axis -1 the first non-singleton dimension is used (columns for a row vector, rows otherwise) and, as in MATLAB, a scalar gives an empty 0-by-0 result.

◆ eig_symbolic

template<typename Scalar >
Matrix<Scalar> eig_symbolic ( const Matrix< Scalar > &  m)
friend

Splits the matrix into its strongly connected (block diagonal) components and solves the characteristic polynomial of each block with poly_roots, so every block may be at most 4-by-4. Larger blocks raise an error. Eigenvalues are assumed real. Returns a column vector; the order follows the block structure, not the magnitude. Only defined for SX; pass SX(m) for a numeric matrix.

>>> evalf(eig_symbolic(SX([[2, 1], [1, 2]])))
DM([1, 3])
>>> M = SX.sym("M", 2, 2)
>>> eig_symbolic(M)
SX(@1=(M_3+M_0), @2=sqrt((sq(@1)-(4*((M_0*M_3)-(M_2*M_1))))), @3=2, [((@1-@2)/@3),
((@1+@2)/@3)])
>>> evalf(eig_symbolic(SX.eye(5) * 3)).T
DM([[3, 3, 3, 3, 3]])

>> a = SX.sym('a'); b = SX.sym('b'); c = SX.sym('c'); d = SX.sym('d');
>> eig_symbolic([a b; c d])
@1=(d+a), @2=sqrt((sq(@1)-(4*((a*d)-(b*c))))), @3=2, [((@1-@2)/@3), ((@1+@2)/@3)]
>> evalf(eig_symbolic(SX.eye(5) * 3))'

◆ einstein [1/2]

template<typename MatType >
MatType einstein ( const MatType &  A,
const MatType &  B,
const MatType &  C,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  dim_a,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  dim_b,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  dim_c,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  a,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  b,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  c 
)
friend

Given two tensors, A and B, computes a third tensor C such that:

C_c = A_a * B_b

With a, b, c representing einstein indices. Instead of the classical index labels i,j,k,... we employ -1,-2,-3,... An index that appears in a or b but not in c is summed over.

A, B, C are represented as CasADi column vectors (column-major flattening), with dim_a, dim_b, dim_c indicating their tensorial dimensions. The product of dim_a must equal the number of elements of A, and likewise for B and C.

In the overload with an explicit C argument, the contraction is added to C.

>>> A = DM([1, 2, 3, 4])
>>> einstein(A, A, [2, 2], [2, 2], [2, 2], [-1, -2], [-2, -3], [-1, -3])
DM([7, 10, 15, 22])
>>> mtimes(DM([[1, 3], [2, 4]]), DM([[1, 3], [2, 4]]))
DM(
[[7, 15],
 [10, 22]])
>>> einstein(DM([1, 2, 3]), DM([4, 5, 6]), [3], [3], [], [-1], [-1], [])
DM(32)


>> A = DM([1; 2; 3; 4]);
>> einstein(A, A, [2, 2], [2, 2], [2, 2], [-1, -2], [-2, -3], [-1, -3])
[7, 10, 15, 22]
>> DM([1 3; 2 4])*DM([1 3; 2 4])
[[7, 15],
 [10, 22]]
>> einstein(DM([1; 2; 3]), DM([4; 5; 6]), 3, 3, [], -1, -1, [])
32


julia> A = ca.DM([1, 2, 3, 4]);
julia> ca.einstein(A, A, [2, 2], [2, 2], [2, 2], [-1, -2], [-2, -3], [-1, -3])

◆ extract

template<typename MatType >
void extract ( std::vector< MatType > &  ex,
std::vector< MatType > &  v,
std::vector< MatType > &  vdef,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
)
friend

Rewrites the expressions ex so that selected intermediate results are replaced by new symbols v with definitions vdef (ex, v and vdef are outputs; in Python the call is extract(ex, opts) -> (ex, v, vdef)). Substituting vdef for v in the result gives back the original expressions. Only nodes that are physically shared in the graph are detected: two separately constructed copies of x+y are distinct nodes (apply cse first to merge them). Not defined for DM.

Options:

  • lift_shared (bool), default true: extract nodes used more than once
  • lift_calls (bool), default false: extract every Function call and its arguments (MX only; SX raises for lift_calls true or lift_shared false)
  • prefix (str), default 'v_', suffix (str), default '', offset (int), default 0: naming of the new symbols

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y")
>>> e = x + y
>>> extract([sin(e), cos(e)])
([SX(sin(v_0)), SX(cos(v_0))], [SX(v_0)], [SX((x+y))])
>>> extract([sin(e), cos(e)], {"prefix": "w_", "offset": 3})
([SX(sin(w_3)), SX(cos(w_3))], [SX(w_3)], [SX((x+y))])
>>> extract([sin(x + y), cos(x + y)])
([SX(sin((x+y))), SX(cos((x+y)))], [], [])
>>> X = MX.sym("X"); Y = MX.sym("Y")
>>> f = Function("f", [X], [sin(X)]); E = X + Y
>>> extract([f(E)*f(E)], {"lift_shared": False, "lift_calls": True})
([MX((v_1*v_2))], [MX(v_0), MX(v_1), MX(v_2)], [MX((X+Y)), MX(f(v_0){0}), MX(f(v_0){0})])


>> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y');
>> e = x + y;
>> [ex, v, vdef] = extract({sin(e), cos(e)});
>> ex{1}, ex{2}, v{1}, vdef{1}

cos(v_0)

(x+y)
>> [ex, v, vdef] = extract({sin(e), cos(e)}, struct('prefix', 'w_', 'offset', 3));

◆ extract_parametric [1/4]

template<typename MatType >
void extract_parametric ( const MatType &  expr,
const MatType &  par,
MatType &  expr_ret,
std::vector< MatType > &  symbols,
std::vector< MatType > &  parametric,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
)
friend

The purpose of extract_parametric is ultimately to save on evaluation time of an expression, by extracting out the parts that are only solely dependent on parameters.

For any: [expr_ret, symbols, parametric] = extract_parametric(expr, par) It holds that: substitute(expr_ret,symbols,parametric) == expr

parametric is only dependant on par expr_ret is not dependant on par, but is dependant on symbols

Example: [expr_ret, symbols, parametric] = extract_parametric((x-sqrt(p))*y+cos(p)**2, p)

expr_ret: (((x-extracted1)*y)+extracted2) symbols: [extracted1, extracted2] parametric: [sqrt(p),cos(p)**2]

Options to control the name of new symbols:

  • offset (int), default 0: Offset for new symbol counter
  • prefix (str), default 'e_': Prefix for new symbols
  • suffix (str), default '': Suffix for new symbols

Option 'extract_trivial' controls the behaviour for extracted parts that consist of pure symbols. If false (default), these parts are not extracted.

expr may also be a list of expressions and par a list of parameter symbols (concatenated internally). An unknown option raises an error. Not defined for DM.

* >>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y"); p = SX.sym("p")
* >>> expr_ret, symbols, parametric = extract_parametric((x - sqrt(p))*y + cos(p)**2, p)
* >>> expr_ret
* SX((((x-e_0)*y)+e_1))
* >>> symbols, parametric
* ([SX(e_0), SX(e_1)], [SX(sqrt(p)), SX(sq(cos(p)))])
* >>> extract_parametric(x*p, p)
* (SX((x*p)), [], [])
* >>> extract_parametric(x*p, p, {"extract_trivial": True})
* (SX((x*e_0)), [SX(e_0)], [SX(p)])
* 

* >> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y'); p = SX.sym('p');
* >> [expr_ret, symbols, parametric] = extract_parametric((x - sqrt(p))*y + cos(p)^2, p);

* >> expr_ret, numel(symbols)
* (x*p)
* 0
* >> opts = struct('extract_trivial', true);
* >> [expr_ret, symbols, parametric] = extract_parametric(x*p, p, opts);
* >> expr_ret, symbols{1}, parametric{1}
* (x*e_0)

◆ fabs

template<typename ExType >

friend

Elementwise; structural zeros are preserved. The unary functions of this group operate on every entry, keep the shape and build a symbolic expression for SX and MX. Those that map 0 to 0 (abs, sqrt, sin, tan, atan, asin, sinh, tanh, asinh, atanh, floor, ceil, sign, erf, erfinv, log1p, expm1) keep the sparsity pattern; the others (cos, cosh, exp, log, log10, acos, acosh, logic_not) return a dense result. Named fabs in Python, where the built-in abs also applies.

DM([1, 0, 2])

◆ fmod

template<typename ExType >
ExType fmod ( const ExType &  x,
const ExType &  y 
)
friend

This Function follows the convention of https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/numeric/math/fmod: the result has the sign of x and magnitude below |y|.

This is equivalent to Python's numpy.fmod and Matlab's rem. It differs from the Python operator x % y on these objects, which follows the Python convention x - y*floor(x/y) (result with the sign of y). Elementwise, shape rules as for plus; structural zeros of x stay zero. A zero divisor gives NaN.

DM([2, 2, -2, -2])
>>> DM([5, 5, -5, -5]) % DM([3, -3, 3, -3])
DM([2, -1, 1, -2])
>>> fmod(SX.sym("x"), 2), SX.sym("x") % 2
(SX(fmod(x,2)), SX((x-(2.*floor((x/2))))))

[2, 2, -2, -2]

◆ graph_substitute [1/4]

MX graph_substitute ( const MX &  ex,
const std::vector< MX > &  v,
const std::vector< MX > &  vdef 
)
friend

Replaces every occurrence of the node v[i] in ex by vdef[i]. Unlike substitute, which only accepts symbolic primitives for v, graph_substitute matches any node, so intermediate results and Function call results can be replaced. Matching is by identity: an expression that was rebuilt (x + y created twice) is a different node and is not matched. Nodes that do not depend on any substituted node are reused, not copied. Shapes of v[i] and vdef[i] must agree.

Parameters
exExpression to substitute in
vNodes to replace
vdefReplacements, same length as v
updatedSet to true if any substitution took place (C++ only)

>>> x = MX.sym("x")
>>> y = MX.sym("y")
>>> s = x + y
>>> e = sin(s) + s
>>> graph_substitute(e, [s], [MX(3)])
MX(3.14112)
>>> graph_substitute(e, [x + y], [MX(3)])
MX(@1=(x+y), (sin(@1)+@1))
>>> try:
...   substitute(e, s, MX(3))
... except Exception as err:
...   print("not symbolic" in str(err))
True
>>> try:
...   graph_substitute(e, [s], [MX.sym("z", 2)])
... except Exception as err:
...   print("Inconsistent shapes" in str(err))
True


>> x = MX.sym('x'); y = MX.sym('y');
>> s = x + y;
>> e = sin(s) + s;
>> graph_substitute(e, {s}, {MX(3)})
3.14112
>> graph_substitute(e, {x + y}, {MX(3)})
@1=(x+y), (sin(@1)+@1)
>> try, substitute(e, s, MX(3)); catch err, disp('not symbolic'); end
not symbolic
>> z = MX.sym('z', 2);
>> try, graph_substitute(e, {s}, {z}); catch err, disp('inconsistent shapes'); end
inconsistent shapes

◆ horzcat [6/6]

template<typename MatType >
MatType horzcat ( const std::vector< MatType > &  v)
friend

Places the matrices side by side, in order: the result has the row count of the inputs and a column count equal to the sum of the column counts. All inputs must have the same number of rows; a 0-by-0 matrix is ignored. The result is of the type of the arguments, numeric arguments are converted to the symbolic type (DM mixes with SX or MX, but SX and MX cannot be mixed). The sparsity pattern of each block is preserved. With no arguments the result is a 1-by-0 matrix.

Alternative terminology: horizontal stack, hstack, horizontal append, [a b]. Inverse of horzsplit: horzcat(horzsplit(x, ...)) == x.

Parameters
vList of matrices with matching row count
Returns
Matrix with the blocks of v side by side

>>> horzcat(DM([1, 2]), DM([3, 4]), DM([5, 6]))
DM(
[[1, 3, 5],
 [2, 4, 6]])
>>> horzcat(SX.sym("x", 2), DM.ones(2, 1))

[[x_0, @1],
 [x_1, @1]])
>>> horzcat(MX.sym("x", 2, 2), MX.sym("y", 2, 0))

template<typename MatType >
MatType if_else ( const MatType &  cond,
const MatType &  if_true,
const MatType &  if_false,
bool  short_circuit = false 
)
friend

Ternary operator, "cond ? if_true : if_false"

Selects if_true where cond is nonzero and if_false elsewhere. cond may be a scalar or have the shape of the branches (elementwise selection); a scalar branch is broadcast. By default the result is if_else_zero(cond, if_true) + if_else_zero(!cond, if_false): both branches are part of the expression and are evaluated, but the value of the unselected branch is discarded, so a nan or inf there does not propagate. With short_circuit true (MX only; ignored for SX and DM) the branches are wrapped in functions and only the selected one is evaluated.

>>> f = Function("f", [x], [if_else(x >= 0, sqrt(x), 0)])
>>> f(-1)
DM(0)
>>> X = MX.sym("X")
>>> if_else(X > 0, X, -X, True)

◆ interp1d

template<typename MatType >
MatType interp1d ( const std::vector< double > &  x,
const MatType &  v,
const std::vector< double > &  xq,
const std::string &  mode,
bool  equidistant = false 
)
friend

The data points are (x[i], v[i, :]): row i of v holds the values at abscissa x[i], so v has as many rows as x has entries and every column is interpolated independently. The result has one row per query point xq[j].

Queries outside the range of x are clamped to the first or last data point (no extrapolation). The result is a constant sparse matrix times v, so for symbolic v the expression is linear in v.

Parameters
xAbscissae, strictly increasing, at least two entries
vData values, x.size()-by-m
xqQuery abscissae, any order
mode"linear" (interpolate), "floor" (value at the data point at or below the query) or "ceil" (at or above); any other string raises an error
equidistantWhen true, x is assumed uniformly spaced and the interval is located arithmetically from x[0] and x[1] instead of by search
Returns
Matrix of size xq.size()-by-m

>>> interp1d([0, 1, 2], DM([0, 10, 20]), [0.5, 1.5])
DM([5, 15])
>>> interp1d([0, 1, 2], DM([0, 10, 20]), [0.5, 1.5], "floor")

>>> interp1d([0, 1, 2], DM([[0, 1], [10, 11], [20, 21]]), [0.5, 2])

template<typename ExType >
bool is_equal ( const ExType &  x,

Depth=0 checks if the expressions are identical, i.e. points to the same node.

a = x*x b = x*x

is_equal(a,b,0) will return false, but is_equal(a,b,1) will return true

Returns a plain boolean, unlike the elementwise comparison eq. With depth > 0 two different nodes are equivalent when they have the same operation and their dependencies are equivalent up to depth-1. ◆ is_linear

template<typename MatType >

const MatType &  var 
)
friend

Defined as: no entry of expr depends on var with order 2 (see which_depends). Only the structure of the graph is inspected, not the values: false negatives are possible (an expression may not be recognised as linear while it really is, e.g. x*x/x). ◆ jacobian

template<typename MatType >
MatType jacobian ( const MatType &  ex,
const MatType &  arg,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
)
friend

The derivative of ex with respect to arg, with both treated as column-major vectors of their elements: the result is ex.numel()-by-arg.numel(), one row per element of ex and one column per element of arg. Entries that are structurally zero are left out of the sparsity pattern.

arg must be symbolic (for MX: symbolic primitives as created by MX.sym, or a concatenation of them; elements of a primitive are rejected). Not defined for DM.

Parameters
optsOptions: "allow_forward" and "allow_reverse" (bool, default true) restrict the AD mode; "symmetric" (bool, default false) hints that the Jacobian is symmetric; "verbose"
Returns
Sparse matrix

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y")
>>> J = jacobian(vertcat(x*y, x**2), vertcat(x, y))
>>> J
SX(
[[y, x],
 [(2.*x), 00]])
>>> J.dim(True)
'2x2,3nz'
>>> A = SX.sym("A", 2, 2)
>>> jacobian(2*A, A).dim()
'4x4'
>>> jacobian(SX(0, 1), vertcat(x, y)).dim()
'0x2'

◆ jtimes

template<typename MatType >
MatType casadi::GenericMatrix< MatType >::jtimes ( const MatType &  ex,
const MatType &  arg,
const MatType &  v,
bool  tr = false,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
)
friend

This is equivalent to mul(jacobian(ex, arg), v) or mul(jacobian(ex, arg).T, v) for tr set to false and true respectively. If contrast to these expressions, it will use directional derivatives which is typically (but not necessarily) more efficient if the complete Jacobian is not needed and v has few rows.

The matrix shapes of ex and arg are kept: v must have the shape of arg (or of ex when tr is true), and several directions can be passed at once by concatenating them horizontally, i.e. v.size2() a multiple of arg.size2(). The result is ex.size1()-by-ex.size2()*n_dir (arg.size1()-by-arg.size2()*n_dir when tr is true). An inconsistent shape of v raises an error.

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y")
>>> ex = vertcat(x*y, x**2); arg = vertcat(x, y)
>>> jtimes(ex, arg, DM([1, 0]))
SX([y, (2.*x)])
>>> jtimes(ex, arg, DM([1, 0]), True)
SX([y, x])
>>> jtimes(ex, arg, DM.eye(2))
SX(
[[y, x],
 [(2.*x), 0]])
>>> jtimes(ex, arg, SX.sym("v", 2))
SX([((y*v_0)+(x*v_1)), ((2.*x)*v_0)])


>> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y');
>> ex = vertcat(x*y, x^2); arg = vertcat(x, y);
>> jtimes(ex, arg, DM([1; 0]))
[y, (2.*x)]
>> jtimes(ex, arg, DM([1; 0]), true)
[y, x]
>> jtimes(ex, arg, DM.eye(2))
[[y, x],
 [(2.*x), 0]]
>> jtimes(ex, arg, SX.sym('v', 2))
[((y*v_0)+(x*v_1)), ((2.*x)*v_0)]


julia> x = ca.SX.sym("x"); y = ca.SX.sym("y");
julia> ex = [x * y; x^2]; arg = [x; y];
julia> ca.jtimes(ex, arg, ca.DM([1, 0]))
SX([y, (2.*x)])
julia> ca.jtimes(ex, arg, ca.DM([1, 0]), true)
SX([y, x])
julia> ca.jtimes(ex, arg, ca.DM.eye(2))

[[y, x],
 [(2.*x), 0]])
julia> ca.jtimes(ex, arg, ca.SX.sym("v", 2))

template<typename Scalar >
void ldl ( const Matrix< Scalar > &  A,

)
friend

Computes A(p, p) = L*diag(D)*L^T with L unit lower triangular. Returns D as a vector, LT holding the strictly upper triangular entries of L^T (the unit diagonal is omitted), and the permutation p. Only the upper triangle of A is referenced. The sparsity pattern of A must be symmetric. Only guaranteed to work for positive definite matrices (no pivoting). Works symbolically on SX.

This function linearizes an expression around a point x0, using x as delta around that point:

◆ low

MX low ( const MX &  v,
const MX &  p,
const Dict &  options = Dict() 
)
friend

For each entry p_i of p, returns the index k such that v[k] <= p_i < v[k+1] for the ascending grid v, clipped to [0, len(v)-2] so that values outside the grid map to the first or last interval. This is the lookup step of linear interpolation. The result has the shape of p and is piecewise constant, so its derivative is zero.

Parameters
vDense ascending grid, vector
pQuery values, dense vector
options"lookup_mode": "linear" (scan), "binary" (bisection), "exact" (assumes an equidistant grid and computes the index arithmetically) or "auto" (default: "binary" for grids longer than 100 entries, else "linear"). Any other key or mode raises an error.

>>> g = MX.sym("g", 4)
>>> p = MX.sym("p", 5)
>>> f = Function("f", [g, p], [low(g, p)])
>>> f(DM([0, 1, 2, 3]), DM([-1, 0, 1.5, 3, 4]))
DM([0, 0, 1, 2, 2])
>>> jacobian(low(g, p), p).nnz()
0
>>> try:
...   low(g, p, {"lookup_mode": "foo"})
... except Exception as e:
...   print("Invalid lookup mode" in str(e))
True


>> g = MX.sym('g', 4); p = MX.sym('p', 5);
>> f = Function('f', {g, p}, {low(g, p)});
>> f(DM([0; 1; 2; 3]), DM([-1; 0; 1.5; 3; 4]))
[0, 0, 1, 2, 2]
>> J = jacobian(low(g, p), p);
>> J.nnz()
0
>> try, low(g, p, struct('lookup_mode', 'foo')); catch e, disp('invalid lookup mode'); end
invalid lookup mode


julia> g = ca.MX.sym("g", 4); p = ca.MX.sym("p", 5);
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [g, p], [ca.low(g, p)]);
julia> f([0, 1, 2, 3], [-1, 0, 1.5, 3, 4])
DM([0, 0, 1, 2, 2])
julia> ca.nnz(ca.jacobian(ca.low(g, p), p))
0
julia> try
           ca.low(g, p, Dict("lookup_mode" => "foo"))
       catch e
           println(occursin("Invalid lookup mode", sprint(showerror, e)))
       end
true

Elementwise comparison; shape rules as for plus. Every comparison in this group returns a matrix of the same type as the operands with entries 1 (true) and 0 (false): for DM a numeric 0/1 matrix, not a boolean, and for SX and MX a symbolic expression that is only decided at evaluation time. ◆ mac

template<typename MatType >
MatType mac ( const MatType &  x,
const MatType &  y,
const MatType &  z,
const std::string &  blas = "reference" 
)
friend

Matrix product of two matrices (x and y), adding the result to a third matrix z. The result has the same sparsity pattern as z, meaning that other entries of the product are ignored. The operation is equivalent to z + project(mtimes(x, y), z.sparsity()). The dimensions of z must match the product, otherwise an error is raised. When x or y is a scalar the result is z + x*y. See mtimes for the meaning of the blas argument.

mtimes is implemented as mac with a structurally zero z of the product pattern.

Parameters
xLeft factor
yRight factor
zMatrix to add to; its sparsity pattern selects the computed entries
Returns
Matrix with the sparsity pattern of z 

>>> A = DM([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
>>> mac(A, A, DM.eye(2))

>>> mac(A, A, DM.ones(2, 2))
DM(
[[8, 11],
 [16, 23]])
>>> mac(MX.sym("x", 2, 3), MX.sym("y", 3, 2), MX.sym("z", Sparsity.diag(2)))
MX(mac(x,y,z))

template<typename ExType >

This Function follows the convention of https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/numeric/math/fmod: the result has the sign of x and magnitude below |y|.

This is equivalent to Python's numpy.fmod and Matlab's rem. It differs from the Python operator x % y on these objects, which follows the Python convention x - y*floor(x/y) (result with the sign of y). Elementwise, shape rules as for plus; structural zeros of x stay zero. A zero divisor gives NaN.

(SX(fmod(x,2)), SX((x-(2.*floor((x/2))))))

[2, -1, 1, -2]

◆ mtimes [1/2]

template<typename MatType >
MatType mtimes ( const MatType &  x,
const MatType &  y,
const std::string &  blas = "reference" 
)
friend

Computes x*y in the linear-algebra sense; the column count of x must equal the row count of y, otherwise an error is raised. When either argument is a scalar the result is the elementwise product instead. The sparsity pattern of the result is the structural product of the patterns (entries that are structurally zero in every term stay structural zeros). For Sparsity arguments only the pattern of the product is computed.

Optional blas selects the BLAS plugin used for dense numeric kernels. The choice only takes effect on numeric DM / MX dense * dense; symbolic types (Sparsity, SX) and the sparse fallback path ignore it.

Values of blas:

  • reference (default): built-in reference kernel (triple loop)
  • classic: whatever BLAS was built into casadi via WITH_LAPACK (typically OpenBLAS)
  • blasfeo: BLASFEO

Plugins (classic, blasfeo) are loaded lazily on first use; if the corresponding plugin DLL isn't present in the build, calling them raises an error.

Parameters
xLeft factor
yRight factor
blasName of the BLAS plugin for dense numeric products
Returns
Matrix of size x.size1() by y.size2()

>>> A = DM([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
>>> mtimes(A, A)
DM(
[[7, 10],
 [15, 22]])
>>> mtimes(A, 2)
DM(
[[2, 4],

>>> mtimes(Sparsity.diag(2), Sparsity.dense(2, 1))

>>> mtimes(MX.sym("x", 2, 3), MX.sym("y", 3, 1))

Finds Z m-by-(m-n) such that AZ = 0 with A n-by-m with m >= n (a matrix with more rows than columns raises an error).

Elementwise comparison; shape rules as for plus. Every comparison in this group returns a matrix of the same type as the operands with entries 1 (true) and 0 (false): for DM a numeric 0/1 matrix, not a boolean, and for SX and MX a symbolic expression that is only decided at evaluation time. ◆ pinv [1/2]

template<typename MatType >
MatType pinv ( const MatType &  A)
friend

If the matrix A is fat (size1<size2), mul(A, pinv(A)) is unity.

pinv(A)' = (AA')^(-1) A

If the matrix A is slender (size1>size2), mul(pinv(A), A) is unity.

pinv(A) = (A'A)^(-1) A'

The normal equations are solved with solve, so A is assumed to have full rank. For a square matrix this is the inverse.

>>> A = DM([[1, 0, 0], [0, 2, 0]])
>>> pinv(A)
DM(
[[1, 0],
 [0, 0.5],
 [0, 0]])
>>> mtimes(A, pinv(A))
DM(
[[1, 0],
 [0, 1]])
>>> pinv(SX.sym("A", 1, 2))
SX(@1=(sq(A_0)+sq(A_1)), [(A_0/@1), (A_1/@1)])


>> A = DM([1 0 0; 0 2 0]);
>> pinv(A)
[[1, 0],
 [0, 0.5],
 [0, 0]]
>> A*pinv(A)
[[1, 0],
 [0, 1]]
>> pinv(SX.sym('A', 1, 2))
@1=(sq(A_0)+sq(A_1)), [(A_0/@1), (A_1/@1)]

template<typename Scalar >
Matrix<Scalar> poly_coeff ( const Matrix< Scalar > &  f,
const Matrix< Scalar > &  x 
)
friend

Returns the coefficients in decreasing power order (highest degree first), as a column vector; the constant term is last. Coefficients may be symbolic in other variables. Found by repeated differentiation, so an expression that is not polynomial in x raises an error. Only defined for SX.

Parameters
exScalar SX expression that is a polynomial in x
xScalar SX symbol

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); a = SX.sym("a")
>>> poly_coeff(3*x**2 + 2*x + 1, x)
SX([3, 2, 1])
>>> poly_coeff((x - a)*(x + a), x)
SX([1, 0, (-sq(a))])
>>> try: poly_coeff(sin(x), x)
... except Exception as e: print("error")
error

◆ poly_roots

p is a dense column vector of coefficients in decreasing power order, as returned by poly_coeff. Closed-form formulas are used for degrees 1 to 4; a zero constant term is split off as a root 0 first. ◆ printme

template<typename ExType >

const ExType &  y 
)
friend

Identity operation with a side effect: whenever the expression is evaluated inside a Function (and hence inside a solver), every nonzero of x is printed on its own line as "|> y : value" in storage (column-major) order, with y an identifier of choice to tell several printme nodes apart. Available as a method x.printme(y) in Python; the derivative is that of x. Use monitor to print a whole matrix at once.

>>> x = MX.sym("x")
>>> f = Function("f", [x], [x.printme(7) * 2])
>>> f(3)

>> f(3)

◆ pw_const

template<typename Scalar >

Builds an SX expression that equals val[0] for t < tval[0], val[k] for tval[k-1] <= t < tval[k] and val[n-1] for t >= tval[n-2], with n = val.numel(). tval must be increasing. valFunction value on each interval, length n

>>> t = SX.sym("t")

>>> try: pw_const(t, [0], [7, 1, 3])
... except Exception as e: print("error")
error

◆ qr

template<typename Scalar >
void qr ( const Matrix< Scalar > &  A,
Matrix< Scalar > &  Q,
Matrix< Scalar > &  R 
)
friend

Factorizes A = Q*R with Q of the same shape as A (orthonormal columns) and R square upper triangular. More stable than classical Gram-Schmidt, but breaks down (nan entries, no error) when the columns of A are (nearly) linearly dependent. A must have at least as many rows as columns. Works symbolically on SX. See J. Demmel: Applied Numerical Linear Algebra (algorithm 3.1). In Python and MATLAB, Q and R are returned as a tuple.

>>> Q, R = qr(DM([[3, 1], [4, 2]]))
>>> Q
DM(
[[0.6, -0.8],
 [0.8, 0.6]])
>>> R
DM(
[[5, 2.2],
 [00, 0.4]])
>>> mtimes(Q, R)
DM(
[[3, 1],
 [4, 2]])
>>> try: qr(DM([[1, 2, 3]]))
... except Exception as e: print("error")
error


>> [Q, R] = qr(DM([3 1; 4 2]));
>> Q
[[0.6, -0.8],
 [0.8, 0.6]]
>> R
[[5, 2.2],
 [00, 0.4]]
>> Q*R
[[3, 1],
 [4, 2]]
>> try, [Q, R] = qr(DM([1 2 3])); catch e, disp('error'); end
error

◆ remainder

template<typename ExType >
ExType remainder ( const ExType &  x,
const ExType &  y 
)
friend

This Function follows the convention of https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/numeric/math/remainder: x - n*y with n the integer nearest to x/y (ties to even), so the result lies in [-|y|/2, |y|/2].

Notably:

  • remainder(5,3) -> -1
  • remainder(5,-3) -> -1
  • remainder(-5,3) -> 1
  • remainder(-5,-3) -> 1

This is equivalent to Python's math.remainder. There is no equivalence in Matlab. Elementwise, shape rules as for plus; structural zeros of x stay zero.

>>> remainder(DM([5, 5, -5, -5]), DM([3, -3, 3, -3]))
DM([-1, -1, 1, 1])
>>> remainder(DM([2.5, 3.5]), 2)
DM([0.5, -0.5])
>>> remainder(MX.sym("x"), 2)
MX(remainder(x,2))


>> remainder(DM([5; 5; -5; -5]), DM([3; -3; 3; -3]))
[-1, -1, 1, 1]
>> remainder(DM([2.5; 3.5]), 2)
[0.5, -0.5]

template<typename MatType >
void separate_linear ( const MatType &  expr,
const MatType &  sym_lin,
const MatType &  sym_const,
MatType &  expr_const,
MatType &  expr_lin,
MatType &  expr_nonlin 
)
friend
Parameters
expr[in]The expression to be separated
sym_lin[in]The symbolic variables w.r.t. which linearity should be checked
sym_const[in]The symbolic variables that are deemed constant
expr_const[out]The constant part of the expression
expr_lin[out]The linear part of the expression
expr_nonlin[out]The nonlinear part of the expression

Every symbol in expr must be listed in sym_lin or sym_const; otherwise an error about free variables is raised.

A post condition is that the following holds: expr = expr_const + expr_lin + expr_nonlin

Here, expr_const is only dependant on sym_const, expr_lin is linear in sym_lin (with coefficients that may depend on sym_const)

Example:

[expr_const,expr_lin,expr_nonlin] = separate_linear(cos(p)+7*x+x*y, vertcat(x,y), p)

expr_const: cos(p) expr_lin: 7*x expr_nonlin: x*y

sym_lin and sym_const may also be lists of symbols. Not defined for DM.

* >>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y"); p = SX.sym("p")
* >>> separate_linear(cos(p) + 7*x + x*y, vertcat(x, y), p)
* (SX(cos(p)), SX((7*x)), SX((x*y)))
* >>> separate_linear(p*x, x, p)
* (SX(0), SX((p*x)), SX(0))
* 

* >> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y'); p = SX.sym('p');
* >> [c, l, n] = separate_linear(cos(p) + 7*x + x*y, vertcat(x, y), p);

* (7*x)
* (x*y)
* >> [c, l, n] = separate_linear(p*x, x, p);
* >> c, l, n

* (p*x)
* 0

◆ solve [1/2]

template<typename MatType >
MatType solve ( const MatType &  A,
const MatType &  b 
)
friend

The solve routine works similar to Matlab's backslash when A is square and nonsingular. The algorithm used is the following:

  1. A simple forward or backward substitution if A is upper or lower triangular
  2. If the linear system is at most 3-by-3, form the inverse via minor expansion and multiply
  3. Permute the variables and equations as to get a (structurally) nonzero diagonal, then perform a QR factorization without pivoting and solve the factorized system.

Note 1: If there are entries of the linear system known to be zero, these will be removed. Elements that are very small, or will evaluate to be zero, can still cause numerical errors, due to the lack of pivoting (which is not possible since cannot compare the size of entries)

Note 2: When permuting the linear system, a BLT (block lower triangular) transformation is formed. Only the permutation part of this is however used. An improvement would be to solve block-by-block if there are multiple BLT blocks.

The description above applies to DM and SX. For MX, triangular systems give dedicated solve nodes, an orthonormal pattern is inverted by transposition, and everything else falls back to solve(A, b, "qr"). A scalar A gives the elementwise division b/A. b may have several columns (one right-hand side each). A non-square A or a row count mismatch raises an error; a numerically singular DM returns nan or inf.

>>> A = DM([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
>>> solve(A, DM([1, 2]))
DM([0, 0.5])
>>> solve(A, DM.eye(2))
DM(
[[-2, 1],

◆ sprank

template<typename MatType >
casadi_int sprank ( const MatType &  x)
friend

The structural rank is the size of a maximum matching between rows and columns of the pattern (via the Dulmage-Mendelsohn decomposition): an upper bound on the numerical rank that depends only on which entries are structurally nonzero, not on their values. A dense matrix always has full structural rank, even when it is numerically singular.

Parameters
xMatrix (or Sparsity); only x.sparsity() is used
Returns
Structural rank, at most min(size1, size2)

>>> sprank(Sparsity.diag(3))
3
>>> sprank(Sparsity.triplet(3, 3, [0, 1, 2], [0, 0, 0]))
1
>>> sprank(DM([[1, 2], [2, 4]]))
2
>>> sprank(DM(2, 3))
0


>> sprank(Sparsity.diag(3))

>> sprank(Sparsity.triplet(3, 3, [0, 1, 2], [0, 0, 0]))
1
>> sprank(DM([1 2; 2 4]))
2
>> sprank(DM(2, 3))
0


julia> ca.sprank(ca.Sparsity.diag(3))

julia> ca.sprank(ca.Sparsity.triplet(3, 3, [0, 1, 2], [0, 0, 0]))
1
julia> ca.sprank(ca.DM([1 2; 2 4]))
2

◆ substitute_inplace

template<typename MatType >
void substitute_inplace ( const std::vector< MatType > &  v,
std::vector< MatType > &  inout_vdef,

)
friend

Substitute variables v out of the expressions vdef sequentially, as well as out of a number of other expressions piggyback

Interprets vdef[k] as the definition of the symbol v[k] and resolves the definitions into each other, so that afterwards neither vdef nor ex contain any of the symbols v. ◆ symvar

template<typename MatType >
std::vector<MatType> symvar ( const MatType &  x)
friend

Returns the symbols the expression was built from, in order of first appearance, each once. For SX every scalar symbol is a separate entry; for MX the entries are the symbolic matrices as created by MX.sym, even if only part of such a matrix is used. Presence in the graph is a structural notion; an expression like 0*x still lists x. Use depends_on for mathematical dependency. Not defined for DM.

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y"); z = SX.sym("z")
>>> symvar(vertcat(z*x, y))
[SX(z), SX(x), SX(y)]
>>> symvar(SX.sym("v", 2)*3)
[SX(v_0), SX(v_1)]
>>> v = MX.sym("v", 2)
>>> symvar(v[0]*3)
[MX(v)]
>>> symvar(SX(3))
[]


>> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y'); z = SX.sym('z');
>> v = symvar(vertcat(z*x, y));
>> numel(v), vertcat(v{:})
3
[z, x, y]
>> v = symvar(SX.sym('v', 2)*3); disp(vertcat(v{:}))
[v_0, v_1]
>> v = MX.sym('v', 2);
>> s = symvar(v(1)*3); disp(numel(s)), disp(s{1})
1
v
>> numel(symvar(SX(3)))
0

◆ taylor [1/2]

template<typename Scalar >
Matrix<Scalar> taylor ( const Matrix< Scalar > &  ex,
const Matrix< Scalar > &  x 
)
friend

Expands ex around a with respect to the scalar symbol x up to the given order: ex(a) + ex'(a)*(x-a) + ex''(a)*(x-a)^2/2! + ... + ex^(order)(a)*(x-a)^order/order! The expansion is done entrywise for a dense matrix ex; sparse ex raises an error. a may itself be symbolic. The two-argument form expands around 0 to first order. Only defined for SX.

Parameters
exDense SX expression to expand
xScalar SX symbol
aScalar expansion point, default 0
orderHighest power of (x-a) kept, default 1; 0 gives ex(a)

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); a = SX.sym("a")
>>> taylor(sin(x), x)
SX(x)
>>> taylor(sin(x), x, a, 1)
SX((sin(a)+(cos(a)*(x-a))))
>>> taylor(exp(x), x, 0, 3)
SX(@1=sq(x), (((1+x)+(0.5*@1))+(0.166667*(@1*x))))
>>> taylor(vertcat(sin(x), cos(x)), x, 0, 2)
SX([x, (1+(-0.5*sq(x)))])


>> x = SX.sym('x'); a = SX.sym('a');
>> taylor(sin(x), x)
x
>> taylor(sin(x), x, a, 1)
(sin(a)+(cos(a)*(x-a)))
>> taylor(exp(x), x, 0, 3)
@1=sq(x), (((1+x)+(0.5*@1))+(0.166667*(@1*x)))
>> taylor([sin(x); cos(x)], x, 0, 2)
[x, (1+(-0.5*sq(x)))]


julia> x = ca.SX.sym("x"); a = ca.SX.sym("a");
julia> ca.taylor(sin(x), x)
SX(x)
julia> ca.taylor(sin(x), x, a, 1)
SX((sin(a)+(cos(a)*(x-a))))
julia> ca.taylor(exp(x), x, 0, 3)
SX(@1=sq(x), (((1+x)+(0.5*@1))+(0.166667*(@1*x))))
julia> ca.taylor([sin(x); cos(x)], x, 0, 2)
SX([x, (1+(-0.5*sq(x)))])

◆ transform [1/4]

template<typename MatType >
MatType transform ( const MatType &  x,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
)
friend

Wraps the expression in a Function of its free symbols, applies Function::transform and re-evaluates it on the original symbols. Each pass is a list starting with a verb: "simplify" (followed by task names), "expand" or "external"; an unknown verb raises an error. Without passes a default set of simplification passes is applied.

>>> transform(x*2*3)
SX((6*x))

◆ vertcat [6/6]

template<typename MatType >
MatType vertcat ( const std::vector< MatType > &  v)
friend

Stacks the matrices on top of each other, in order: the result has the column count of the inputs and a row count equal to the sum of the row counts. All inputs must have the same number of columns; a 0-by-0 matrix is ignored. Type and sparsity rules are those of horzcat. With no arguments the result is a 0-by-1 matrix.

Column vectors stack cheaply; for MX, stacking matrices with more than one column is rewritten as a horizontal concatenation of the transposes.

Alternative terminology: vertical stack, vstack, vertical append, [a;b]. Inverse of vertsplit: vertcat(vertsplit(x, ...)) == x.

Parameters
vList of matrices with matching column count
Returns
Matrix with the blocks of v stacked vertically

>>> vertcat(SX.sym("x", 2), 3)
SX([x_0, x_1, 3])
>>> vertcat(DM([[1, 2]]), DM.eye(2))
DM(
[[1, 2],
 [1, 00],
 [00, 1]])
>>> vertcat(MX.sym("a", 2, 3), MX.sym("b", 1, 3))
MX(horzcat(a', b')')
>>> vertcat().shape
(0, 1)
>>> vertcat(MX.sym("a", 2, 2), MX.sym("b", 2, 3))
Traceback (most recent call last):

horzcat(a', b')'

...vertcat dimension mismatch...

◆ vertsplit [2/2]

template<typename MatType >
std::vector<MatType > vertsplit ( const MatType &  x,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  offset 
)
friend

Returns the row blocks x[offset[i]:offset[i+1], :], in order. The offsets must start at 0, be non-decreasing and end at the number of rows of x, otherwise an error is raised. Each block carries the corresponding part of the sparsity pattern. The offsets of a list of matrices that were stacked with vertcat can be recovered with offset. Inverse of vertcat: vertcat(vertsplit(x, offset)) == x.

Parameters
xMatrix (or Sparsity) to split; any shape
offsetStart row of every block followed by the row count of x
Returns
List of matrices of the same type as x, one per block

>>> x = SX.sym("x", 5)
>>> vertsplit(x, [0, 2, 5])
[SX([x_0, x_1]), SX([x_2, x_3, x_4])]
>>> parts = [DM.ones(2, 1), DM.ones(3, 1)]
>>> vertsplit(x, offset(parts))
[SX([x_0, x_1]), SX([x_2, x_3, x_4])]
>>> vertsplit(DM([[1, 2], [3, 4]]), [0, 1, 2])
[DM([[1, 2]]), DM([[3, 4]])]

◆ which_depends

template<typename MatType >
std::vector<bool> which_depends ( const MatType &  expr,
const MatType &  var,
casadi_int  order,
bool  tr 
)
friend

Structural dependency check by sparsity propagation, without forming derivatives. With order 1, an entry depends if the corresponding Jacobian entry is structurally nonzero; with order 2, if it enters nonlinearly (second derivative structurally nonzero). Operations whose derivative is structurally zero, such as floor or sign, count as not depending.

Parameters
exprExpression
varSymbolic expression
order1 or 2; other values raise an error
trWhen false, the result has one entry per element of var: does any element of expr depend on it. When true, one entry per element of expr: does it depend on any element of var.
Returns
List of booleans

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y")
>>> e = vertcat(x*y, x**2, 3*x)
>>> which_depends(e, vertcat(x, y), 1, False)
[True, True]
>>> which_depends(e, vertcat(x, y), 1, True)
[True, True, True]
>>> which_depends(e, vertcat(x, y), 2, True)
[True, True, False]


>> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y');
>> e = vertcat(x*y, x^2, 3*x);
>> which_depends(e, vertcat(x, y), 1, false)
1 1
>> which_depends(e, vertcat(x, y), 1, true)
1 1 1
>> which_depends(e, vertcat(x, y), 2, true)
1 1 0
